en: The *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* states that contemplating the mind may be called "attainment. Furthermore, it is asked:

Previously, it was said that true suchness, buddha-nature, and all meritorious qualities have awakening as their root; however, it remains to be examined how ignorance and the mind of all evils [relate to this].
"What serves as its root?

He replied, "Although the mind of ignorance possesses eighty-four thousand afflictions, passions, and desires, as well as immeasurable and boundless multitudes of evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
To state the essentials:
all [afflictions] take the three poisons as their root.
These three poisons are namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
These three poisons of the mind are themselves capable of encompassing all evils.
It is like a great tree: although its root is but one, the branches and leaves it produces are immeasurable in number.
From those three roots of poison, all manner of evil karmas arise;
they exceed the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times, beyond all analogy.
In this way, the mind itself acts as the three poisons within its own fundamental substance.
If the six sense organs manifest, they are also called the "six thieves.
These six thieves are what are known as the six consciousnesses;
they enter and exit the various sense organs, greedily clinging to the myriad objects of the world.
Because they are able to produce evil karma and damage the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*),
they are called the "six thieves.
All sentient beings, due to these three poisons and the six thieves, [suffer].
Deluded and agitated in body and mind, they sink into the cycle of birth and death,
transmigrating through the six realms and undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, there are rivers whose source is small, yet whose meandering streams flow without ceasing.
Thus it can spread out in waves and billows for ten thousand *li*;
yet if someone were to cut off its source,
then all the currents would cease.
Those seeking liberation eliminate the three poisons and the six thieves;
thus, they are able to remove all sufferings for themselves. Again, it was asked:
"The three realms and the six destinies are vast and boundless."
If one contemplates only the mind, how can one avoid that suffering? The answer is:
The karmic retributions of the three realms are produced solely by the mind.
Fundamentally, if there were no mind, there would be no three realms.
The three realms are identical to the three poisons.
Greed constitutes the desire realm;
hatred constitutes the form realm.
Delusion constitutes the formless realm.
Because these three minds aggregate the retributions of various evil karmas and bring about the incomplete cycle of saṃsāra,
they are called the "three realms."
Furthermore, because karma created through the three poisons varies in weight, the realms of rebirth are distinct, leading to six different destinations;
therefore, they are called the "six destinies" (*ṣadgati*). Question:
How are these divided into six based on lightness and heaviness? Answer: [As follows:]
If there are sentient beings who do not understand the true cause and, with deluded minds, practice wholesome deeds,
they will not yet escape birth within the three realms in the three inferior destinies.
What are these three inferior destinies?
They all cultivate the ten wholesome deeds while falsely seeking happiness;
yet they cannot avoid the realm of craving and are reborn within the six destinies.
Although they fully uphold the five precepts, they give rise to false feelings of attachment and aversion;
thus, they have not yet escaped the realm of anger and are reborn in the human realm.
Deludedly clinging to the conditioned and seeking blessings through heterodox means,
they fail to escape the realm of ignorance and are reborn as asuras.
Seeing these three categories is called the "threefold heaviness.
What are the threefold heavinesses?
They are as follows: to give rein to the three poisons of mind and perform only evil deeds.
They fall into the three lower realms:
those whose karma of greed is heavy fall into the realm of hungry ghosts;
those whose karma of hatred is heavy fall into the realm of hell-beings.
Those whose karma of delusion is heavy fall into the realm of animals.
Thus, these three heavy types, combined with the three preceding light types, result in the six realms of existence.
Therefore, one should know that all wholesome karma arises from the mind itself.
"Simply by being able to collect the mind and remain free from all deviant evils, the karma of saṃsāra within the three realms and six destinies will naturally be extinguished.
To be able to extinguish all sufferings is what is called liberation. He asked again:
As the Buddha has said:
"I attained the path of Buddhahood after immeasurable diligent suffering over three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas.
How is it that you now say that merely eliminating the three poisons is called liberation? Answer: [As follows:]
That which the Buddha spoke of as the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is, in fact, the mind of the three poisons.
*Asaṃkhyeya* in the Hu language means "incalculable" in the Han language.
These three poisonous minds, within a single thought-moment, constitute everything.
"Ganges-sands" refers to that which is incalculable.
Since the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is already shrouded and obstructed by the three poisons,
if one does not transcend those three Ganges-river-sands of poisonous and evil thoughts, [one cannot realize it].
What is meant by "attaining liberation"?
It is that one is now able to eliminate the three poisons of the mind—greed, hatred, and delusion;
this is what is called having crossed over and attained [liberation] after three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Sentient beings of the final age are ignorant and dull-witted;
failing to understand the Tathāgata’s three kinds of incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) secret teachings,
they consequently claim that the end of the kalpa has already arrived.
Is it not the case that one who practices with doubt and awakening does not regress from Bodhi before finally attaining the Buddha-way?
Now, you require students to merely contemplate the mind and not cultivate the practice of precepts;
how can this constitute a valid means of goodness?
As for "assemblage" (skandha):

because one can restrain the three poisons, there are three measures of goodness that universally assemble within the mind; therefore, it is called the "threefold aggregate precept" (tri-skandha-śīla).
As for "pāramitā": [it means]...
This is the Sanskrit term;
in the Han language, it means "reaching the other shore.
Because the six sense faculties are pure and unstained by worldly dust.
That is to say, one can emerge from afflictions and reach the shore of Bodhi;
therefore, they are called the six pāramitās. Furthermore, it was asked:
"As stated in the sūtras..."
The three clusters of pure precepts consist of the vow to sever all evil and the vow to cultivate all good.
"One vowed to deliver all sentient beings;
now you speak of restraining the three poisons of the mind.
Is this not a contradiction between the text and its meaning? The answer is:
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are words of truth;
they must be without error.
When a bodhisattva was practicing asceticism during past causes, he...
Regarding the poison of greed, one vows to sever all evils and constantly cultivates ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Regarding the poison of hatred, one vows to cultivate all virtues and thus constantly cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the poison of delusion, one vows to deliver all sentient beings and thus constantly cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*).
By upholding these three kinds of pure dharmas— namely, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
one is able to transcend the evil karma of the three poisons and thereby attain Buddhahood.
For by restraining the three poisons, all evils are extinguished.
Therefore, it is called "severance.
Because one can uphold the three precepts, all virtues are fully perfected;
thus, one is named a Buddha.
Because one who practices what can sever [afflictions] achieves the myriad deeds,
benefiting both self and others and universally rescuing all sentient beings,
it is called "crossing over" (pāramitā).
Since one knows that the precepts one cultivates are not separate from the mind, if the mind itself is pure, all meritorious virtues will likewise be pure. It is further said:
"If you wish to attain the purity of the Buddhas, you should purify your own mind."
"As the mind is purified, so is the Buddha-field purified.
If one can restrain the three types of poisonous minds, the three clusters of pure precepts will naturally be accomplished. It is further said:
As stated in the sūtras,
the six pāramitās are also called the six perfections (ṣaḍ-pāramitā),
namely: giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Now, regarding the statement that the purification of the six sense organs constitutes the six *pāramitās*, how are these two to be harmonized?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the "six perfections"? Answer:
One who wishes to cultivate the six *pāramitās* must purify the six sense organs; one who wishes to purify the six sense organs must first subdue the six thieves.
One who can abandon the thief of the eye and,
free from all attachment to the realm of forms, remains without regret or stinginess is said to be capable of giving;
one who can restrain the thief of the ear is likewise so named.
To not allow oneself to be heedless regarding the sensory object of sound is called upholding the precepts;
it is able to eliminate the thief of the nose.
To be masterful in balancing various fragrances and odors with equanimity and flexibility is called patience;
it is the ability to restrain the thief of the tongue from craving perverse flavors.
To recite, praise, and expound upon the teachings without a mind of weariness is called diligence;
it is able to subdue the thief of the body.
When the mind remains serene and unmoving amidst all sensory contacts and desires,
it is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
it is able to restrain the thieves of the mind.
To not follow ignorance while constantly cultivating awakening wisdom and delighting in all meritorious virtues is called "wisdom.
Furthermore, "crossing over" (du) means "transporting.
The six *pāramitās* are like boats and rafts, capable of transporting sentient beings to reach the other shore.
Therefore, they are called the Six Perfections. Furthermore, it was asked:
"Regarding what was said concerning Śākyamuni Tathāgata when he was a bodhisattva—that he once drank three pecks and six liters of milk gruel before attaining the Way of the Buddha—[how is this so?]"
"This means that having first consumed milk as a cause, one subsequently realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
How could it be that liberation is attained through the contemplation of the mind alone?
He replied, "It is exactly as you have said; there is no falsehood in this."
One must certainly consume milk before one can attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha said, "I ate milk.
There are two kinds of milk.
That which the Buddha consumes is not the impure milk of the world,
but rather the pure Dharma-milk of True Suchness (Tathatā).
The three pecks represent the threefold pure precepts (tri-śikṣāpada-viśuddhi-śīla).
The "six pints" refers to the six *pāramitās*.
When attaining the Way of the Buddha, one partakes of such;
it is through this milk of the Dharma that one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
If one says that the Tathāgata consumes the impure, pungent, and raw milk of cows produced through worldly sexual union,
would this not constitute a most grievous slander of the Dharma?
The Tathāgata is himself the indestructible, stainless *dharmakāya* of vajra;
having forever transcended all worldly sufferings,
why should he require such impure milk to satisfy his hunger and thirst?
As it is said: the ox does not dwell on high plateaus, nor in low-lying marshes;
it does not eat grain, wheat, dregs, husks, or beans.
He does not herd with ordinary oxen;
his body is the color of purple-polished gold.
It is said that this ox is none other than Vairocana Buddha.
Out of great kindness and great compassion, and out of pity,
[the Buddha] nourishes all sentient beings who seek liberation with the subtle Dharma-milk of the three clusters of pure precepts and the six pāramitās within his own pure essence.
In this way, the milk that is pure within suchness is not something the Tathāgata drinks to achieve enlightenment.
If all sentient beings were to eat it, they would all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. He asked again:
As stated in the sutras,
the Buddha said:
"Sentient beings construct monasteries, cast images, burn incense, scatter flowers, and light perpetual lamps."
By circumambulating stupas and practicing walking meditation throughout the six periods of day and night, observing the fast, and performing prostrations,
all such various merits lead to the realization of the Buddha-way.
If one contemplates the mind alone, it universally encompasses all practices.
"Such matters must be false. He replied:
"The Buddha has taught through immeasurable skillful means;
yet all sentient beings have dull faculties and narrow, inferior capacities."
Because the profound is difficult to grasp, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is provisionally illustrated by means of the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
If one does not practice internally but seeks only externally,
hoping thereby to obtain merit, [one will fail].
This is impossible.
As for the term "Gārāma," it is a Sanskrit word from the Western lands (India).
This stage is translated as the Stage of the Pure Abode.
If one eternally eliminates the three poisons and constantly purifies the six sense faculties,
the body and mind will be serene and pure both internally and externally.
This is what is called the cultivation of a *sugata*.

Furthermore, as for those who cast images, these are representations of the Tathāgata created by all sentient beings seeking the Buddha-way as they cultivate various practices of awakening; how could it be that [the Buddha] dispatched the casting of works in gold or copper?

Therefore, those who seek liberation take the body as the furnace, the Dharma as the fire, wisdom as the craftsman, and the three clusters of pure precepts and the six pāramitās as the design patterns.
Smelting and refining the body and mind into the Buddha-nature of True Suchness (Tathatā),
one enters universally into the molds of all precepts,
practicing according to the teachings without any deficiency or omission.
The image of the true countenance is spontaneously accomplished.
That which is achieved is the ultimately eternal, subtle, and wondrous form-body (*rūpakāya*), not a conditioned phenomenon subject to decay.
If a person seeks the Way but does not understand this, [they will fail].
If one has thus cast a true image, on what basis can one claim to have accomplished meritorious virtue?
Furthermore, as for the burning of incense,
it is not the kind of incense characterized by worldly forms.
This is indeed the fragrance of the unconditioned True Dharma.
It permeates all defiled and evil karmas, causing them entirely to be purified and extinguished.
This fragrance of the True Dharma has five essential natures.
The first is the fragrance of ethical discipline (*śīla-gandha*),
which means being able to sever all evils and cultivate all virtues.
The second is the fragrance of meditative concentration (*samādhi-gandha*).
The so-called "fragrance of resolute faith" refers to a mind that has no regression regarding the Mahāyāna.
The third is the "fragrance of wisdom," which refers to constantly observing the internal and external aspects of one's own body and mind.
The fourth is the fragrance of liberation,
which is said to be able to sever all fetters of ignorance.
The fifth is the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
What is called "awakened awareness" (bodhi) constantly penetrates the obstruction of ignorance.
Such five fragrances are peerless in the world.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, he commanded his sons to burn these priceless incenses with the fire of wisdom as an offering to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
At this time, sentient beings are ignorant and of dull faculties;
they do not understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata,
but merely take external fire to burn the worldly, obstructive fragrances of agarwood, sandalwood, and incense.
How can one hope to obtain the fruits of merit?
Furthermore, the meaning of scattering flowers is likewise this:
it refers to preaching the True Dharma, which is called the flower of merit.
Benefiting sentient beings by sprinkling [its fragrance] upon all,
it universally bestows adornment upon the nature of suchness;
this flower of merit is praised by the Buddhas.
It is ultimately eternal and constant, with no period of decay or decline.
Furthermore, if there are those who scatter such flowers, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
If the Tathāgata causes sentient beings to cut and trim silken fabrics, [they likewise gain great benefit].
Furthermore, it is impossible for one to damage plants and trees to make them into scattered flowers. Why is this so?
One who upholds the pure precepts does not allow themselves to transgress against the myriad phenomena of the great earth;
even if they should inadvertently transgress, they incur a grave offense.
How much more so for one who now intentionally violates the prohibitions and harms all things while seeking a reward of merit?
"To seek benefit and instead suffer loss—how could such a thing exist? He asked again:
"As for the lamp—"
Awakening is the awakening of the upright mind.
Wisdom, being clear and luminous, is metaphorically described as a lamp.
Therefore, all who seek liberation should always take the body as the lampstand.
The mind is the lamp-vessel;
faith is the wick;
and the increase of various virtuous conducts serves as the added oil.
Wisdom is clear and penetrating, comparable to a lamp that burns constantly.
In this way, the lamp-light of the true awakening of suchness destroys all the darkness of ignorance and delusion,
and is able to use this Dharma to successively awaken others.
This is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps;
as the lamps continue one after another, the light never ends.
Because it is inexhaustible, it is called "Ever-Burning Light."
In the past, there was a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara;
the meaning is likewise so.
Foolish sentient beings do not understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of skillful means.
Devotedly practicing falsehood and clinging to the conditioned,
they then light a lamp of ghee or oil in the world to illuminate a single room, claiming this to be "relying on the teachings.
Is this not a grave error?
Why is this? The Buddha emitted a ray of light from the single hair-tuft between his eyebrows,
which shone upward, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds.
If the radiance of one’s own body illuminates the ten directions universally,
how could such worldly lamps as these possibly provide benefit?
Upon careful examination of this principle, it must be that they cannot.
Furthermore, regarding those who practice the Way during the six periods:
within the six sense faculties, they constantly practice the Buddha-way at all times;
"way" (dao) means awakening.
This refers to cultivating various practices of awakening to subdue the six sense faculties;
practicing pure conduct over a long period without abandoning it is called "practicing the path during the six periods.
A *stūpa* (塔) is the body.
Constantly causing awakening and wisdom to circulate through the body and mind, without ceasing for even a single thought-moment,
is called "circumambulating the stupa.
The noble monks of the past practiced the Way in this manner and attained nirvana.
Those who seek liberation do not understand this principle.
What is called "practicing the Way"?
I observe that nowadays those beings of dull faculties have never practiced internally, but instead cling solely to external seeking.
To take this obstructive body and circumambulate the stupas of the world,
running to and fro day and night, is merely to exhaust oneself in vain;
it provides no benefit whatsoever to true nature.
How truly pitiable is the extreme gap between delusion and awakening!
Furthermore, those who observe the fast must ensure they grasp its true meaning;
otherwise, their benefit will be merely nominal and their efforts in vain.
"Zhai" (fasting) means "to align.
It refers to aligning the body and mind so as not to allow them to become distracted.
"Chi" (maintaining) means "to protect."

What is called the practice of precepts according to the Dharma requires that one must guard and maintain them by restraining the six sense-faculties, subduing the three poisons, and diligently observing and purifying body and mind.
To understand this meaning is what is termed "fasting" (upavāsa).
Furthermore, there are five kinds of those who observe the fast:
the first is those who subsist on the food of Dharma-joy.
The first is to joyfully practice in accordance with the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
The second is the food of dhyāna-joy,
which refers to the physical and mental bliss resulting from the internal and external realization of tranquility.
Third is the food of mindfulness,
which means constantly maintaining mindfulness of all Buddhas such that mind and speech are in accord.
Fourth is the food of aspiration.
The so-called food of conduct consists in constantly seeking virtuous aspirations while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Fifth is the food of liberation,
which means that the mind is always pure and untainted by worldly dust.
This pure food is called the food of the fast (upavāsa-bhakta).
If there were someone who did not eat these five kinds of pure food while outwardly observing the fast, such a thing would be impossible.
Regarding what is called "this food":
if one recites [the scripture] in reverse concerning the food of ignorance and evil karma,
how can one who breaks their fast obtain merit?
There may be those who are ignorant and deluded, failing to comprehend this principle;
their bodies and minds are dissolute, they commit every kind of evil,
and they indulge their lustful desires with total lack of shame or remorse.
To merely abstain from external food while claiming to observe the fast—
how is this different from seeing a rotting corpse and claiming it still possesses life?
It is a matter that reveals one's inevitable death.
Furthermore, as for prostration,
it should be performed in accordance with the Dharma;
one must necessarily internalize the principle and, through clear illumination, investigate and adapt to each specific circumstance.
The principle is eternally non-abandoning;
phenomena have their times of manifestation and concealment.
To realize this meaning is what is called "acting in accordance with the Dharma."
Ritual propriety (*li*) is reverence.
Prostration is that which is performed for this purpose:
to manifest the true nature of reverent respect and to subdue ignorance.
It is for the purpose of prostration.
Because of reverence, one does not dare to damage [the body];
because of submission, one does not allow it to run wild or become unrestrained.
If one can forever sever evil thoughts and maintain virtuous mindfulness at all times,
then even if no physical form is perceived, it is still called prostration.
As for its ritual method, it is the very manifestation of the body itself.
In order to cause those in the mundane world to manifest a humble mind,
one must subdue the external mind and display an appearance of reverence;
when this is employed, it becomes manifest.
If one abandons them, they are concealed.
To perceive clarity externally while being internally awakened is what constitutes correspondence.
If, however, one does not practice according to the principle of the Dharma and merely clings to the gate of phenomena, one remains within the realm of the mundane.
Though they indulge in greed and delusion and constantly commit evil deeds,
outwardly they manifest empty physical forms and perform nameless prostrations.
Lacking shame before the noble ones and even deceiving the ordinary folk,
one cannot avoid falling into ruin.
"How can one achieve merit?
Since there is nothing to be attained, how does one rescue the Way? He asked again.
In the *Kaṃsapaṭṭa-sūtra*,
it is stated that bathing the community of monks yields immeasurable merit.
By what principle or dharma does this merit first come to fruition?
If one asks whether it is appropriate to contemplate only the mind:
the answer is that the term "Saṃgha" does not refer to worldly conditioned phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Jentāka-sūtra for his disciples.
Desiring to cause others to receive and uphold the method of ritual bathing,
he therefore employs worldly affairs as metaphors for the True Doctrine.
As for the explanation of the seven matters:
First, pure water;
second, kindling a fire;
third, cleansing powder.
Fourth, willow twigs;
fifth, pure ash;
sixth, clarified butter.
Seventh is the undergarment.
These seven items are used as metaphors for seven dharmas.
By means of these seven dharmas, all sentient beings may bathe and adorn themselves, thereby removing the defilements of the three poisons and ignorance.
As for those seven dharmas:
the first is to purify the body and mind through pure precepts,
just as clear water washes away all dust and grime.
The second refers to the observation of the internal and external through wisdom,
just as lighting a fire can warm water.
The third refers to discernment and rejection.
Just as soap powder can remove dirt and grease,
the fourth is the true severance of all false speech;
it is like chewing a willow twig, which can eliminate bad breath.
The fifth refers to having correct faith and being free from doubt,
just as one who has rubbed their body with ash can avoid the wind.
The sixth refers to being gentle and harmonious toward those who are harsh and stubborn.
Just as ointment and oil permeate and soften the skin,
the seventh is shame and remorse for all evil deeds;
it is like undergarments that conceal an ugly form.
The seven dharmas mentioned above are all the secret meanings within the sutras.
The Tathāgata established them for those of sharp faculties who follow the Mahāyāna,
not for ordinary persons of small wisdom and inferior capacity.
This is why people are unable to awaken to or understand it.
That "warm bathhouse" is none other than this very body.
For this reason, the fire of wisdom provides warmth, and the bath of pure precepts washes away [defilements] from within the Buddha-nature; by upholding these seven dharmas, one adorns oneself.
At that time, the bhikṣus, being clever and of sharp intelligence, all awakened to the holy intent.
By means of this, one achieves the merit of spiritual practice and merely attains the fruits of sainthood; however,
the sentient beings of the present age are ignorant and of dull faculties.
The matter was unfathomable;
he used worldly water to wash his physical body,
yet he claimed to be acting in accordance with the sutras.
Is this not awakening?
Furthermore, for instance, Buddha-nature is not an ordinary form;
the dust of afflictions is originally without marks.
How could one possibly use obstructed water to wash the unconditioned body?
This is inconsistent with reality;
how could it ever be possible?
If one says that the body is pure despite its obstructions,
one should contemplate this body as being produced without cause from the impurity of desire,
replete with stench and filth.
It is filled within and without.
If one seeks purity by washing this body, it is like washing a ditch until the mud is exhausted; then one must stop.
Judging by this evidence, it is clear that external washing was not taught by the Buddha. Again, he asked:
"The sutras state that if one recollects the Buddha with a sincere heart, one will certainly attain liberation. He replied:
Now, as for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha,
they must ensure that their mindfulness is correct;
if it does not accord with the definitive meaning, it is erroneous.
With right mindfulness, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land;
how could one reach it with wrong mindfulness?
"Buddha" means awakening.
That which is called "awareness" (覺察) means not allowing evil to arise from the source of the mind.
"Mindfulness" (念) means recollection;
it refers to firmly maintaining the practice of the precepts, being diligent and unwavering, and thoroughly understanding the meaning of the Tathāgata.
This is called right mindfulness.
Thus we know that mindfulness resides in the mind and not in words.
One seeks the fish by means of the trap.
Having caught the fish, one forgets the trap;
having sought the meaning through words,
one forgets the words once the meaning is attained.
Since it is called "recollection of the Buddha," one must practice the substance of that recollection;
if the mind lacks reality, [it cannot be so].
To recite empty words with the mouth and vainly contemplate hollow efforts—
what benefit or accomplishment can there be?
Furthermore, as for "reciting" (song) and "mindfulness" (nian),
their names and meanings differ significantly.
That which is uttered by the mouth is called reciting.
That which resides in the mind is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Thus, one knows that mindfulness arises from the mind;
it is termed the gateway to awakening and practice.
To recite [the mantra] within the mouth is merely the characteristic of sound;
to grasp at such characteristics while seeking merit will ultimately yield nothing.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All that has marks is entirely false and illusory.
It further says:
If one sees me by means of form,
or seeks me by means of sound,
such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Observing it in this way, one realizes that phenomenal appearances are not the ultimate truth;
the merits cultivated by the Buddhas of the past were all based on internal realization and not merely external discourse. This alone is the correct teaching.
The mind is the source of all that is good and the master of all that is evil.
*Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Constant joy arises from one's own mind;
the six realms of the cycle of birth and death within the three worlds originate from the mind.
The mind is the gateway to transcending the world.
The mind is the opening channel for liberation.
For one who knows the gateway, how could they worry that realization is difficult to achieve?
For one who has opened the channel, what cause for concern is there regarding failure to reach the goal?
I have observed that those of shallow understanding in the present age devote themselves solely to the construction of images and stupas as their meritorious deeds;
they squander vast amounts of wealth and precious materials, accumulating them extensively on land and in water,
engaging in vain projects and needlessly conscripting laborers.
Stacking wooden blocks and piling up mud, they paint reds and greens;
with all their heart and strength, they delude themselves and others,
yet remain unaware of shame.
When have they ever awakened to see that their diligent attachment is merely to speak of signlessness while remaining as dull-witted as those lost in confusion?
They merely crave the small compassion of the present moment, unaware that they will enter into great suffering in the future.
This practice of cultivation merely exhausts oneself;
turning one's back on the correct path to return to the heterodox, one falsely claims to have attained merit.
One should simply be able to collect the mind and illuminate within, so that contemplation and discernment are constantly clear.
Cut off the three poisons so that they may forever perish;
do not allow the six thieves to cause further intrusion or disturbance.
Thus, one will naturally be adorned with the various merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Innumerable Dharma gates are all fully accomplished.
Transcending the mundane and realizing the holy, the direct witness is not far off;
awakening occurs in an instant—why trouble yourself with white hair?
The dharma-gate is profound and secret; how could it be fully set forth?
I shall discuss its essence in brief and explain a small portion of it in detail.
*Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*, one fascicle, recorded on the twenty-third day of the fifth month in the year of Gengshen.
